title: 3 Popular Strategies You Should Stop Using With Difficult Students -with-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies three widely used but counterproductive strategies for handling difficult students: intimidation, persuasion, and capitulation. He explains that intimidation produces only temporary compliance while breeding private resentment and distrust. Persuasion—pulling students aside to explain or convince—interferes with genuine accountability and pushes students to either parrot answers or shut down. Capitulation, or simply giving up on enforcing standards, sends the devastating message that a student isn't worth the effort. He argues the real path forward is doing less, not more: removing these three habits rather than adding new interventions.
points: Intimidation (yelling, threats, scolding) produces only temporary improvement while building private resentment that undermines trust.
Persuasion, or trying to talk students into behaving, interferes with genuine accountability and causes defensiveness or rehearsed compliance.
Capitulation—picking battles or letting misbehavior slide—communicates that a student is beyond hope, deepening the problem.
All three strategies increase the alienation and 'differentness' that difficult students already feel.
Improvement comes not from piling on new interventions but from eliminating these three ineffective habits.
quotes: Much of your success with difficult students hinges on what you don’t do.
Any strategy that seeks to frighten or bully students into behaving will backfire every time.
Trying to convince students to behave entails telling them what they should think and how they should feel.
Picking your battles, letting misbehavior go, caving in . . . capitulation amounts to giving up on difficult students.
Holding them to a standard of behavior they need for success in school is the most compassionate thing you can do for them.
No, the secret isn’t in what you have to do. It’s in what you don’t have to do.
